edition.title: P100 NEWS + CULTURE + SCIENCE & TECH + SPORT
edition.deck: A political attack in Australia, a landmark Kenyan verdict and aid cuts in Gaza lead a day of international and domestic developments.
edition.editorialNote: Prioritises consequential developments and fresh reporting. Returning coverage of France, Ukraine and the Canadian base fire is included only where this gather adds a meaningful update or distinct dimension.

content.headline: Australian MP Helen Haines critically injured in apparent deliberate attack
content.shortHeadline: Australian MP critically injured in apparent attack
content.standfirst: Helen Haines was struck by a car outside her constituency office in Victoria. Police are investigating whether it was intentional; the prime minister says it appears to have been a deliberate act, but the motive is not known.

image.caption: Helen Haines, an independent MP and anti-corruption campaigner.

sources.originalTitle: Australian MP critically injured after being hit by car in apparent attack
What we know about apparent attack on Australian MP hit by car
Australsk politiker har kritiske skader efter muligt angreb

segments.body: Independent MP Helen Haines, 65, is critically ill in hospital after being hit by a car outside her office in Wangaratta, in the state of Victoria. A 43-year-old man was detained at the scene and later arrested. Police say a knife was found in the vehicle.

segments.title: An investigation is under way
segments.body: Victoria Police say they are investigating whether the incident was intentional and do not believe there is an ongoing threat to the community. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese called it a deliberate act, but said it was too early to understand the motive. Counter-terrorism police are involved.

content.headline: Kenyan pastor convicted of murdering 191 people in starvation cult case
content.shortHeadline: Kenyan pastor convicted over deaths of 191 people
content.standfirst: Paul Mackenzie and 29 other cult leaders were found guilty of murder, most of the victims children. The verdict is the first on the most serious charges in a case linked to more than 400 bodies found in Shakahola forest.

image.caption: Paul Mackenzie led a church that attracted thousands of followers.

sources.originalTitle: Kenya pastor convicted of ordering parents to starve their children to death

segments.body: A Kenyan court has found self-proclaimed pastor Paul Mackenzie guilty of murdering 191 people, all but one of them children. Prosecutors said he instructed followers to starve their children so they could “meet Jesus”. Twenty-nine other leaders of the cult were also convicted; all had pleaded not guilty.

segments.title: A case among several
segments.body: Authorities say more than 400 bodies were found in shallow graves in Shakahola forest, where Mackenzie led followers. He and other leaders face further cases, including charges related to terrorism and radicalisation. Many of the dead remain unidentified.

content.headline: World Food Programme cuts Gaza food aid as funding runs short
content.shortHeadline: Gaza food aid cut by a third as WFP faces funding gap
content.standfirst: The UN agency says it will reduce the number of people it helps from 1.6 million to 1.1 million as winter approaches. It says the cuts reflect a funding shortfall, not lower needs or lack of access.

image.caption: Dalal al-Dahdouh said her family's food handouts were insufficient even before the cuts.

sources.originalTitle: Funding shortages force World Food Programme to cut aid to Gaza

segments.body: The World Food Programme says funding shortages will force it to reduce assistance in Gaza by about a third, from 1.6 million people to 1.1 million. Daily hot meals from community kitchens will fall from 250,000 to 150,000, while some families in hard-to-reach areas will receive meals every other day.

segments.title: A worsening strain on families
segments.body: The WFP says its Palestinian operations received less than half the funding they had in previous years and it urgently needs $450m for the next six months. Its Palestine director said the reductions were due to finances, “not because the needs are coming down, or because we don't have access”. Families interviewed by the BBC said the aid they already received was insufficient.

content.headline: Ukraine says US gave no warning before Russian strike on Kyiv power plants
content.shortHeadline: Kyiv says US warning did not come before Russian strikes
content.standfirst: Ukraine says it received no advance warning before a Russian missile barrage hit power plants in Kyiv, reviving tensions over US support. Washington has not confirmed the reason; Secretary of State Marco Rubio cited a possible software problem in an earlier incident.

image.caption: Workers repair railway tracks at a Kyiv metro station hit by an overnight Russian missile strike.

sources.originalTitle: US gave us no warning of Russian strikes on Kyiv power plants, Zelenskyy says
Ukraine war briefing: Trump accuses Zelenskyy of not wanting to end war as feud rumbles on
Trump says suspension of Russia sanctions is to keep peace negotiations going

segments.body: Ukrainian officials say the country received no US warning before a Russian missile barrage hit power plants in Kyiv overnight. President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said there had again been no warning from partners. Ukraine says it did receive a warning before a later strike.

segments.title: Dispute over US support
segments.body: The missed warning comes amid a public dispute between Zelenskyy and Donald Trump, who paused a new sanctions package against Russia and said he wanted to keep Moscow at the negotiating table. Rubio said a software problem had affected an early-warning system on an earlier night and that US European Command was looking into the strikes. US officials had not publicly cited such a fault before.

content.headline: France calls for local curfews after police admit losing control in some cities
content.shortHeadline: France considers local curfews after violent protests
content.standfirst: The prime minister has asked regional authorities to consider partial curfews as officials review security failures after weekend unrest. A separate market sell-off has pushed French borrowing costs close to a 24-year high.

image.caption: Police and protesters during unrest in France.

sources.originalTitle: French prime minister calls for ‘local and partial’ curfews after riots
Katya Adler: France's government under pressure after weekend of widespread violence
France hit by debt sell-off as violent protests unnerve investors

segments.body: Prime Minister Sébastien Lecornu says he has asked regional authorities to impose “local and partial” curfews if needed, while ruling out a full curfew across cities such as Paris. Interior Minister Laurent Nuñez acknowledged a “lack of anticipation” and said police had lost control in some places. President Emmanuel Macron has ordered a security review.

segments.title: Unrest rattles markets
segments.body: The Guardian reported that France's 10-year bond yield rose as much as 16 basis points to 4.94% on Monday, bringing borrowing costs close to a 24-year high. Analysts cited the risk that political instability could make it harder for the government to cut spending and reduce its debt.

content.headline: Alberta votes on whether to begin legal process for separation referendum
content.shortHeadline: Alberta votes on whether to start separation process
content.standfirst: Voters are being asked whether the province should begin the legal steps needed for a future binding referendum on independence—not whether to leave Canada now. The gather contains no result from Monday's vote.

image.caption: Albertans vote on whether to start the legal process for a separation referendum.

sources.originalTitle: Why is Alberta voting on whether to separate from Canada, and how likely is it to happen?

segments.body: Alberta's vote asks whether the provincial government should start the constitutional process required to hold a binding referendum on separation. A “yes” would not itself make Alberta independent. The province is also voting on nine other questions, including proposals on immigration and constitutional powers.

segments.title: A disputed path to the ballot
segments.body: The vote follows a push for a separation referendum in the oil-rich province. A court blocked a citizen-led petition after ruling that First Nations had not been consulted; the provincial government appealed. A separate petition opposing separation gathered more than 400,000 signatures. The gather provides background and polling, but no result from Monday's vote.

content.headline: Four soldiers died as fire swept through Canadian military training base
content.shortHeadline: Fire killed four at Canadian base and spread within seconds
content.standfirst: Military officials say high winds drove flames a kilometre in 30 to 60 seconds during live-munitions training in Alberta. The cause remains under investigation, and officials say the death toll and 39 injured include people in critical condition.

image.caption: Canadian Forces Base Wainwright, where a fast-moving fire killed four service members.

sources.originalTitle: Deadly fire at Canada military base moved a kilometre 'in 30 to 60 seconds'
What we know so far about deadly fire at Canadian military base
Four die in Canadian military base fire – everything we know

segments.body: Four Canadian service members are confirmed dead after a fire at Canadian Forces Base Wainwright in Alberta. Officials say 39 people were taken to hospital, at least 19 in critical condition. Maj-Gen Wade Rutland said the flames travelled a kilometre in 30 to 60 seconds after the wind shifted.

segments.title: Investigation continues
segments.body: The fire began near a training area where infantry were using live munitions. Rutland said officials knew about a fire on the base for several hours and that training was allowed to continue “for a certain amount of time”; it is not yet known what started the blaze. Officials have ruled out terrorist activity and say the investigation may take at least a month.

content.headline: Storm floods parts of Spain and moves towards southern France
content.shortHeadline: Deadly storm brings severe flooding to Spain and France
content.standfirst: At least two women died after heavy rain flooded towns on Spain's eastern coast, where some areas received more than 600mm in 48 hours. The slow-moving storm is bringing further warnings for France and could affect Italy and Croatia.

image.caption: Floodwaters inundate towns in Spain as Storm Adam moves towards France.

sources.originalTitle: Voldsomt uvejr rammer Spanien og Frankrig - mindst to er døde

segments.body: At least two women have died after being caught in floodwaters in eastern Spain, according to local authorities cited by Reuters. Spain's meteorological institute says some areas received more than 600mm of rain in 48 hours, the highest amount there since 1987. Helicopters have rescued people from rooftops.

segments.title: Warnings extend east
segments.body: Storm Adam is moving slowly across the Mediterranean towards southern France. Forecasts warn of further heavy rain, including up to 300mm in parts of Marseille over 12 hours. Spain has also issued warnings for the south and islands; the system is expected to move east, with Italy and Croatia potentially affected.

content.headline: Scientists and MPs call for inquiry into unequal health impacts of air pollution
content.shortHeadline: 150 urge inquiry into unequal health impacts of air pollution
content.standfirst: A letter to Prime Minister Andy Burnham says lower-income areas and minority-ethnic communities face greater exposure. Campaigners also point to hospital admissions for breathing difficulties among children in several English areas.

image.caption: A view of a city street, illustrating the pollution exposure raised by campaigners.

sources.originalTitle: Burnham urged to launch inquiry into unequal health impacts of air pollution

segments.body: A letter signed by 150 scientists, MPs and campaigners is urging the government to investigate the unequal health effects of air pollution. Institute for Fiscal Studies research cited in the report found persistently higher pollution in lower-income areas in England, and exposure about 6% higher for minority-ethnic populations than for white populations.

segments.title: Children among those affected
segments.body: Data obtained by Mums for Lungs through freedom-of-information requests recorded more than 200,000 hospital or A&E visits for breathing difficulties among children in 11 English cities and areas in 2025, including over 120,000 involving babies and toddlers. The Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs says air quality is improving overall, but that further action is needed.

content.headline: Plan for 15,780 homes in Norfolk Broads faces environmental challenge
content.shortHeadline: Norfolk Broads housing plan challenged over pollution risks
content.standfirst: A Labour MP has asked the environment watchdog to intervene over a scheme that would allow nearly 16,000 homes in a protected area. Critics say its restoration measures would leave much of the added nutrient pollution unaddressed; Natural England says the plan aims to protect habitats while enabling development.

image.caption: The Norfolk Broads, where a new plan would allow housing development in a protected area.

sources.originalTitle: Stop ‘cash to trash’ housebuilding in Norfolk Broads, says Labour MP

segments.body: The first environmental delivery plan under the government's planning reforms would allow 15,780 homes in the Norfolk Broads. Developers would contribute £42m to a nature restoration fund. Natural England says the development would cause harm through pollution and other effects, while the plan proposes conservation measures in return.

segments.title: Critics say pollution remains
segments.body: Labour MP Chris Hinchliff has urged the Office for Environmental Protection to intervene, arguing that the plan does not address enough nitrogen and phosphorus pollution and omits measures such as septic-tank upgrades. The government and Natural England say the approach is based on evidence and aims to protect habitats while allowing sustainable development. The consultation closes on 31 October.

content.headline: Russell Brand rape trial hears woman's account of alleged 2004 attack
content.shortHeadline: Court hears woman's account in Russell Brand rape trial
content.standfirst: A woman told police she was assaulted at a Soho bar after meeting the comedian in 2004, the court heard. Brand denies all charges and has pleaded not guilty.

image.caption: Russell Brand arrives at Southwark Crown Court.

sources.originalTitle: Russell Brand had ‘maniacal grin’ as he dragged woman into toilet and raped her, court told

segments.body: Jurors at Southwark Crown Court heard a pre-recorded police interview in which a woman alleged Russell Brand grabbed her and dragged her into a toilet at a Soho bar in 2004, where she said he raped her. The woman told police she had met him about a minute earlier.

segments.title: Brand denies the charges
segments.body: Brand, 51, faces three charges of rape, three of sexual assault and one of indecent assault relating to six women and alleged incidents between 1999 and 2009. He denies all the charges and has pleaded not guilty. The court heard that his barrister challenged the woman's account.

content.headline: Tommy Robinson denies harassment charges as trial opens
content.shortHeadline: Tommy Robinson denies threatening journalists
content.standfirst: Prosecutors say the far-right activist used messages and social-media posts that made two MailOnline journalists fear for their safety. Robinson denies both charges.

image.caption: Tommy Robinson arrives at Southwark Crown Court for the start of his trial.

sources.originalTitle: Tommy Robinson used ‘bullyboy, intimidatory tactics’ to threaten journalists, court told

segments.body: The harassment trial of Tommy Robinson, whose real name is Stephen Yaxley-Lennon, has opened at Southwark Crown Court. He is charged with two counts of harassment causing fear of violence against journalists Andrew Young and Jacob Dirnhuber. He denies both charges.

segments.title: Prosecution outlines allegations
segments.body: Prosecutors allege Robinson sent threatening messages and posted images of the journalists' homes on X, prompting them and their families to fear for their safety. The opening statement also said he could have complained to a press regulator instead. The allegations have not been tested in court.

content.headline: Residents face six years of scaffolding as cladding work awaits approval
content.shortHeadline: London residents wait six years for cladding work to start
content.standfirst: Residents of a north London block say scaffolding has blocked light and created security fears, but cladding repairs have yet to begin. The building owner says work cannot start until the safety regulator approves it.

image.caption: Natasha Dyett says scaffolding blocks natural light from her home in Archway Heights.

sources.originalTitle: ‘We’re living in darkness’: six years of scaffolding, still no post-Grenfell cladding

segments.body: Archway Heights has been covered in scaffolding for more than six years, but cladding work has not begun. Residents say metal panels block light from windows and that people have used the scaffolding to enter the building. One resident said a man stood outside her bedroom window after climbing the structure.

segments.title: A contested approval process
segments.body: The building's owner, Places for People, says it cannot start work until the Building Safety Regulator approves it. The regulator says an application submitted in 2024 was invalid and a later one required further information. Places for People says CCTV is operational and an alarm system is being progressed; residents say alarms have not worked.

content.headline: Parents say upfront childcare costs make work harder under universal credit
content.shortHeadline: Childcare payment rules leave some working parents in debt
content.standfirst: Research finds many parents using universal credit childcare support struggle with upfront nursery bills and delays in reimbursement. Researchers propose a single system that would remove upfront payments.

image.caption: Parents using universal credit childcare support say upfront bills can make it difficult to work more hours.

sources.originalTitle: The parents ‘better off’ on universal credit due to childcare trap

segments.body: Parents receiving universal credit can claim back 85% of childcare costs, but must pay first. Some say they have used credit cards or cut their working hours because they cannot meet the upfront bills. In research shared with The i Paper, nearly half of parents using the support said it did not enable them to work extra hours.

segments.title: Researchers propose a single offer
segments.body: The Early Education and Childcare Coalition and the Centre for Analysis of Social Exclusion recommend replacing separate childcare schemes with one offer that removes upfront payments and covers the poorest families' costs. They say a gradual withdrawal as income rises could be introduced without extra public spending. The Department for Work and Pensions says it has taken steps to help with upfront costs.

content.headline: Rogue roofers took £61,000 from pensioner, daughter says
content.shortHeadline: Daughter says roofing scammers took her father's £61,000
content.standfirst: A gang convicted over a £1m fraud operation targeted Michael Cooper with doorstep offers of home repairs, his daughter says. Citizens Advice says suspected roofing scams were its most common reported fraud involving goods and services last year.

image.caption: Nicola Lamb with her father, Michael Cooper, who was targeted by a home-repair scam.

sources.originalTitle: Cowboy builders scammed my dad of £61,000 – then his life fell apart

segments.body: Michael Cooper paid £61,000 to a group that offered roofing and other home repairs, according to his daughter, Nicola Lamb. National Trading Standards, which was investigating the gang, alerted the family. Cooper had recently received an early Alzheimer's diagnosis and later died, aged 86; his daughter says the shock of learning about the fraud changed his life.

segments.title: A wider warning
segments.body: Twenty-two people linked to the operation were sentenced in September. The group extracted more than £1m through unnecessary, poor-quality or overpriced work, the report says. Citizens Advice found suspected roofing scams made up 10% of goods-and-services complaints flagged as fraud, and advises people to be wary of unsolicited offers and to get work agreements in writing.

content.headline: The Canary announces indefinite closure amid dispute over its finances
content.shortHeadline: The Canary news site announces indefinite closure
content.standfirst: The leftwing outlet says attacks and financial pressure made its position unsustainable. Former staff have disputed its account, citing alleged mismanagement; its chief executive says employees and freelancers were paid up to date as of 30 September.

image.caption: The Canary says it is closing for the foreseeable future.

sources.originalTitle: The Canary news website announces closure after ‘vicious campaign against us’

segments.body: The Canary, founded in 2015, says it is closing indefinitely after what it describes as “multiple attacks” and “malicious lies” that made its position unsustainable. It has also cited difficulty accessing funds after Lloyds Bank blocked a substantial amount of its money earlier this year.

segments.title: Competing accounts of the crisis
segments.body: Some journalists at the outlet say the banking issue distracted from wider financial mismanagement and allege that more than £2m in summer funding was spent on unsuccessful projects. Chief executive Steve Topple says permanent employees were paid up to date and that pension contributions and freelancer payments were current as of 30 September.

content.headline: Danish study finds TikTok can recommend misogynistic content within minutes
content.shortHeadline: TikTok feeds can surface manosphere content within minutes
content.standfirst: Researchers found that fictional profiles built around ordinary interests such as dating and fitness were quickly recommended misogynistic videos. The study does not establish that exposure changes young people's views, and TikTok says it removes most content that breaks its rules.

image.caption: A phone displaying TikTok, the platform examined in the report.

sources.originalTitle: Unge mænds feed flyder over med kvindefjendsk indhold: De eksponeres næsten dagligt
Særligt to interesser risikerer at trække unge mænd ind i manosfærens loop
Unge mænd møder kvindefjendsk indhold efter få minutters scrolling

segments.body: A Danish report says young men can encounter content from the manosphere—online material that denigrates women or promotes limiting their rights—in ordinary TikTok feeds. Researchers testing fictional profiles based on young men aged 16 to 19 found it took an average of three minutes for such content to be recommended.

segments.title: Exposure is not the same as endorsement
segments.body: The study also analysed viewing histories from 29 young men and found five to six identifiable manosphere videos a week on average, but said the sample was not representative and the total may be an underestimate. Researcher Kenneth Reinicke cautioned that exposure does not necessarily change attitudes. TikTok says it proactively removes 98.1% of videos that violate its rules on hate and hateful conduct.

segments.title: Dating and fitness feeds
segments.body: The report identifies dating and fitness as interests that can lead to more manosphere recommendations, while a gaming-focused profile received none in the test. Researchers and the minister urge parents to discuss what young people encounter; the report does not show that every young man who sees this material adopts its views.

content.headline: Copenhagen police ask watchdog to investigate blows to photographers
content.shortHeadline: Police refer photographer assault allegations to watchdog
content.standfirst: The photographers, from Ekstra Bladet and Politiken, say officers struck them at separate demonstrations on Saturday. Copenhagen Police has asked the Independent Police Complaints Authority to investigate; the authority says it has not yet received formal complaints.

image.caption: Demonstrators at a Copenhagen protest where photographers later reported being struck by police.

sources.originalTitle: Københavns Politi beder DUP om at undersøge slag mod fotografer

segments.body: Copenhagen Police has asked the Independent Police Complaints Authority to investigate two reported incidents in which photographers were struck by police during demonstrations on Saturday. Politiken says its photographer was hit several times with a baton and had his camera broken; Ekstra Bladet's photographer said he was struck on the arm.

segments.title: Formal complaints pending
segments.body: Both newspapers have said they will complain, and press photography and journalist organisations have asked police leadership how it will prevent a repeat. The complaints authority told DR it had not yet received specific complaints about Saturday, while police said it would submit the case.

content.headline: One in three teachers report abusive language from pupils in recent survey
content.shortHeadline: Teachers report frequent abusive language from pupils
content.standfirst: In a new survey, a third of responding teachers said pupils had used offensive language towards them in the past week, and four in ten said it happened daily or more. The report does not provide enough detail here to judge how representative the responses are.

image.caption: Archive image illustrating the survey's focus on teachers and pupils.

sources.originalTitle: "Hvis du skriver hjem, så smadrer jeg dig" – ny lærerundersøgelse vækker bekymring

segments.body: A survey for the education publication Folkeskolen found that one in three responding teachers had experienced abusive language from pupils in the previous week. Four in ten said it happened daily or several times a day. Six in ten said pupils' language had grown harsher over the past five years.

segments.title: A wider concern about school conditions
segments.body: Psychologist and former teacher Rasmus Alenkær said the findings pointed to schools in crisis, while also noting that pupils' behaviour may reflect unmet needs and instability in the classroom. The report refers to earlier findings on violence between pupils and falling academic results, but the gather does not provide the survey's sample size or methodology.

content.headline: Regions seek access to patient records so ambulance crews can learn
content.shortHeadline: Regions want ambulance crews to review patient records
content.standfirst: Danish Regions is asking the health minister to change the law so ambulance personnel can review records after treating patients. The proposal is framed as a way to improve care, but would require strict privacy safeguards.

image.caption: An ambulance in Denmark, where regions want crews to review some patient records.

sources.originalTitle: Søren redder liv til hverdag, men han aner ikke, hvordan det går patienterne

segments.body: Danish Regions wants ambulance personnel to be able to review the records of patients they have treated, so they can learn whether their assessment and care were appropriate. At present, the law gives access to patient records to professions including doctors, nurses, dentists and midwives, but not ambulance personnel.

segments.title: Privacy safeguards
segments.body: The proposal will be sent to the health minister by Christoffer Buster Reinhardt, chair of the regions' health committee. Ambulance doctor Allan Bach says access would help staff improve, while arguing that they should face the same strict restrictions as other healthcare professionals and that misuse would have consequences.

content.headline: Cyclist injured on disputed road as calls for Holbæk bike path grow
content.shortHeadline: Cyclist injured as residents press for delayed bike path
content.standfirst: Heidi Sørensen suffered a broken elbow after a car hit her from behind on Hvalsøvej near Smidstrup. Holbæk and Lejre have agreed to build a cycle path, but work has not started despite funding in Holbæk's budget.

sources.originalTitle: Kvinde blev slynget af cyklen og landede på mark – nu kommer hendes mand med opråb

segments.body: Heidi Sørensen was hit from behind by a car while cycling to work on Hvalsøvej near Smidstrup, in Holbæk municipality. She suffered a bruised eye and a broken elbow and was taken to hospital. Her husband says residents have been seeking a cycle path on the road for years.

segments.title: Funding, but no start date
segments.body: Holbæk's 2026–29 budget sets aside 6.5 million kroner for a cycle path, and the two municipalities have agreed to establish one. The work has not begun. A municipal director told TV 2 East that a cycle path is needed, but the report gives no start date for construction.

content.headline: Danish publisher will keep selling Sally Rooney's books amid UK dispute
content.shortHeadline: Danish publisher keeps Sally Rooney books on sale
content.standfirst: Gutkind says the author does not break Danish law by donating royalties to Palestine Action, which is on Britain's proscribed terror list. The legality of that listing is due to return to court in the UK in November.

image.caption: Sally Rooney's novels are to remain on sale in Denmark.

sources.originalTitle: 'Krænker ikke nogen dansk lov': Forlag fortsætter salg af bøger trods støtte til organisation på britisk terrorliste

segments.body: Danish publisher Gutkind says it will continue publishing Sally Rooney's books in Denmark. Its chief executive says Rooney does not break Danish law by choosing to donate royalties from her books to Palestine Action, which is proscribed as a terrorist organisation in Britain.

segments.title: UK legal challenge continues
segments.body: The proscription has faced competing court rulings in Britain, and the case is due before the UK Supreme Court in early November. Gutkind says it is concerned that the British restriction limits publication of books that are not themselves unlawful. The report says the United States has also designated Palestine Action a terrorist group.

content.headline: Danish experts call for drug tests for learner drivers
content.shortHeadline: Experts propose drug tests for learner drivers
content.standfirst: Substance-treatment workers and driving instructors say some young people take lessons with drugs still in their blood. They want testing during training, but the report presents this as a proposal, not an agreed policy.

sources.originalTitle: Unge tager kørekort med narko i blodet

segments.body: A substance-treatment therapist, a driving instructor and a representative of driving instructors say they have encountered cases or concerns involving learner drivers with drugs in their blood. They argue that the effects can persist after the person no longer feels intoxicated, creating a safety risk during a lesson.

segments.title: Who would pay?
segments.body: The therapist proposes testing students once or twice during their driving course, and the instructors' representative is open to the idea. He questions who should pay, saying learners already face high costs. The Road Safety Council warns that residual drugs can still affect driving, but the report does not provide prevalence data or any government decision on testing.

content.headline: Danish influencer council suspends work without handling a case
content.shortHeadline: Influencer council pauses after handling no complaints
content.standfirst: The voluntary body, set up with 810,000 kroner from the Danish Journalists' Union, is going into what its chair calls dormancy after attracting only 200 influencer members. Supporters say firms and creators failed to back its standards.

image.caption: An expert says the influencer council is difficult to call a success.

sources.originalTitle: Influencernævn lukker og slukker for nu: Har ikke ført en eneste sag

segments.body: The Danish influencer council is suspending its work after handling no complaints in its first year. The Journalists' Union spent 810,000 kroner establishing it. About 200 influencers signed up to its voluntary ethical guidelines, far short of the broader industry participation its organisers had hoped for.

segments.title: Standards without enforcement
segments.body: The council's chair says there was too little support from influencers and the companies that use them. The guidelines and website will remain, but the chair says there will be no body with the capacity to enforce the rules. An advertising executive called the closure a setback for an industry that wants to be treated seriously.

content.headline: Michael Kiwanuka’s Fudge is rough-edged, lush and full of life
content.shortHeadline: Michael Kiwanuka’s Fudge finds life in the rough edges
content.standfirst: Recorded alongside Small Changes but made in a different spirit, Kiwanuka’s delayed album is a vivid, melodic work in its own right. Its reflections on musical uncertainty resonate differently after his stroke.

image.caption: Michael Kiwanuka recording Fudge.

sources.originalTitle: Michael Kiwanuka: Fudge review – rough and instinctive, but also lush and alive with melody

segments.body: Fudge began as a set of jams recorded alongside Michael Kiwanuka’s 2024 album Small Changes, but it sounds less polished and more immediate. Tape hiss, abrupt starts and extended playing give it a live-in-the-studio feel, while lush strings and memorable melodies make the songs feel carefully shaped rather than rough for roughness’ sake.

segments.title: A different resonance
segments.body: Kiwanuka’s release was delayed after he had a stroke and spent months in hospital; he said he was putting the record out because he did not know how long it would be before he could release another. Songs that dwell on his future in music now carry an added weight, though the review hears an artist who sounds sure of what he wants to do.

content.headline: Cameron Winter’s Carnegie Hall album turns a live night into something lasting
content.shortHeadline: Cameron Winter makes a live night feel like a new beginning
content.standfirst: The Geese frontman’s solo recording pares his songs back to voice and piano, revealing new qualities in familiar material and introducing three unreleased songs from a career-making performance.

sources.originalTitle: Live at Carnegie Hall

segments.body: On Live at Carnegie Hall, Cameron Winter reshapes songs from Heavy Metal with just his voice and piano. The review hears the spaces between notes opening up, turning one song that once moved with a small, plodding click track into something that glides. Three unreleased songs from the concert add to the sense of an evening with its own momentum.

segments.title: A performance becoming a record
segments.body: The album and its accompanying concert film preserve Winter’s December 2025 Carnegie Hall performance, where filmmaker Paul Thomas Anderson and Benny Safdie appeared onstage with a camera. The review sees the recording as more than a document: the songs seem to outgrow the circumstances of their creation and take on the stature of standards.

content.headline: Rachel Chinouriri’s second album finds a sharp voice in romantic chaos
content.shortHeadline: Rachel Chinouriri makes emotional messiness feel like pop
content.standfirst: On i think i spoke too soon, Chinouriri’s conversational songwriting meets a shinier sound. The review finds her most compelling when goofy romantic drama and genuine vulnerability occupy the same song.

sources.originalTitle: I think I spoke too soon

segments.body: Rachel Chinouriri’s second album is her most polished, pairing her familiar alt-rock and pop instincts with brighter, more synth-heavy production. The smoother sound sometimes competes with her voice, but the review says the record finds its stride when arcade-like details and guitars frame her funny, unsettled account of young love.

segments.title: The charm of the contradiction
segments.body: Songs such as “I’m a star” and “AAAHHH!!!” let Chinouriri play up the drama without losing the feeling underneath it. The review argues that her emotional instincts make her more than another relatable pop persona: her insecurity and self-awareness sound convincing whether she is joking or letting the hurt show.

content.headline: KOOL FAITH / LOOSIES II turns a shoegaze band’s network into a mixtape
content.shortHeadline: TAGABOW’s mixtape opens up its wide-ranging musical world
content.standfirst: They Are Gutting a Body of Water bring more than a dozen collaborators into a 29-track set that moves between shoegaze, footwork, folk and rap, while also showcasing the Philadelphia label Julia’s War.

sources.originalTitle: KOOL FAITH / LOOSIES II

segments.body: KOOL FAITH / LOOSIES II takes its mixtape logic seriously: the 29 tracks draw in artists from the Julia’s War roster and beyond, with the sound shifting from Hotline TNT’s sustained guitars to a footwork collaboration with DJ Manny and laid-back rap over emo-tinged loops. The review hears a band widening its palette without losing its own identity.

segments.title: A community in the music
segments.body: The compilation also connects the label’s emerging artists with better-known collaborators. Greg Mendez’s folk melodies swell into distortion, while Horse Jumper of Love’s slowcore is pushed into a more urgent register. Rather than hiding behind a compilation, the review suggests, TAGABOW stand alongside artists they admire and invite listeners into their wider musical community.

content.headline: Worldpeace DMT make playful, carefully built pop on Stick Around for Tea
content.shortHeadline: Worldpeace DMT find feeling beneath their playful pop
content.standfirst: Leo Fincham and Rowan Please scale back the sampling sprawl of their debut for songs that play with the tension between childhood and adulthood, irony and earnestness.

sources.originalTitle: Stick Around for Tea

segments.body: Stick Around for Tea finds Worldpeace DMT making more room for songs than for the collage of sounds on their debut. Their finely assembled pop combines slinky strings, stray rattles and electronic textures, with Rowan Please’s playful delivery and Leo Fincham’s synthetic, sometimes bass-like voice pulling in different directions.

segments.title: Is the joke sincere?
segments.body: The album’s schoolroom theatricality invites listeners to wonder whether the duo mean what they sing. The review argues that the question is part of the point: childlike playfulness and adult understanding meet in songs that can sound like nursery rhymes one moment and finely wrought expressions of longing the next.

content.headline: Jess Williamson’s A Mile South of Heaven finds her at home in country
content.shortHeadline: Jess Williamson turns distance into intimate country songs
content.standfirst: Produced by Shooter Jennings, Williamson’s sixth album works through her ties to Texas and Los Angeles without forcing a choice between them. The review hears her most assured songwriting yet.

sources.originalTitle: A Mile South of Heaven

segments.body: On A Mile South of Heaven, Jess Williamson moves further into country, with pedal steel, fiddles and a natural Texas twang replacing much of the indie-rock sheen of earlier work. The songs keep returning to the distance between Texas and Los Angeles, making each place a source of longing as well as a place to leave.

segments.title: A voice that carries history
segments.body: The review praises Williamson’s phrasing and songwriting for making small details feel lived-in. In songs such as “Country Mile” and “The Gem and Mineral Show”, the narrator’s perspective shifts, turning familiar country themes of restlessness into a more searching account of becoming oneself and facing what follows you.

content.headline: You Can See Everything turns Elizabeth Holmes into an unsettling mystery
content.shortHeadline: Elizabeth Holmes remains an enigma in You Can See Everything
content.standfirst: Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim’s documentary has earned strikingly strong reviews, but its close access to Holmes does not settle the question of how she understands her own fraud conviction.

image.caption: Elizabeth Holmes outside court in San Jose in 2022.

sources.originalTitle: 'As famous and defiant as ever': Why Theranos founder Elizabeth Holmes remains the US's most fascinating fraudster
The reviews are in! Is You Can See Everything the greatest film ever?

segments.body: The documentary follows Elizabeth Holmes, her partner and their young children in the weeks before she reported to prison for defrauding investors in Theranos. She insists that she never lied and that the company’s blood-testing device worked; the film juxtaposes her account with Nathan Fielder’s visible scepticism and, later, another voice that questions whether he may be too caught up in her story.

segments.title: Acclaim, without a verdict
segments.body: The Guardian report notes the film’s exceptional early review scores and box-office opening in the US and Canada. The BBC account, drawing on the filmmakers’ festival remarks, describes a documentary that leaves competing explanations open: Holmes may be deliberately manipulative, or she may genuinely believe her own claims. Neither account presents that puzzle as resolved.

content.headline: A 1972 Harlem reunion brings Renaissance artists back into the room
content.shortHeadline: A Harlem Renaissance reunion, rediscovered on film
content.standfirst: Once Upon a Time in Harlem restores footage of a 1972 gathering of writers, artists and musicians who helped shape the Harlem Renaissance. Their lively disagreements become part of the film’s record of a movement and its legacy.

image.caption: Guests at the Harlem Renaissance reunion filmed for Once Upon a Time in Harlem.

sources.originalTitle: ‘They were brilliant people’: fascinating film reveals a Harlem Renaissance reunion

segments.body: Filmmaker William Greaves invited surviving figures of the Harlem Renaissance to a 1972 gathering at the Duke Ellington House and filmed their conversations. His granddaughter Liani Greaves and son David have shaped the material into a 100-minute documentary, restoring footage from a much larger archive and keeping the focus on the party and its guests.

segments.title: A movement, not a monolith
segments.body: The guests remember their work and argue over how the Renaissance should be understood. Romare Bearden challenges historian Nathan Huggins over the place of visual artists in his account, while the presence of George Schuyler draws visible disapproval. The filmmakers see those differences as evidence of a community with shared ambitions, not a single point of view.

content.headline: Fatherland finds Thomas Mann caught between postwar Germany’s divides
content.shortHeadline: Fatherland puts Sandra Hüller at the heart of a family crisis
content.standfirst: Paweł Pawlikowski’s restrained monochrome drama follows Thomas Mann’s 1949 return to Germany, where public recognition cannot quiet private grief or resolve the political ambiguity of his homecoming.

image.caption: Sandra Hüller as Erika Mann and Hanns Zischler as Thomas Mann in Fatherland.

sources.originalTitle: Fatherland review – Sandra Hüller brings a bayonet of intelligence to Paweł Pawlikowski’s taut return

segments.body: Thomas Mann returns from exile to a divided Germany, accepting honours in both Frankfurt and the communist East German city of Weimar. As he tries to stand above the political divisions, his daughter Erika, played by Sandra Hüller, grieves for her brother Klaus and challenges the cost of her father’s distance.

segments.title: The cost of standing apart
segments.body: The review sees the family story as inseparable from Mann’s public choices. His attempt to avoid taking sides is unsettled by Klaus’s writing and by the news that reaches the family during the tour. Pawlikowski’s controlled, monochrome film offers little consolation, framing survival and cultural belonging as questions rather than answers.

content.headline: The Night Is Fading Away turns a cinema into a refuge in Argentina
content.shortHeadline: A cinema becomes a refuge in The Night Is Fading Away
content.standfirst: After budget cuts push a projectionist into a night-watchman role, a single-screen cinema becomes a home for people on the margins. The film connects their shared refuge to political action in the wake of Javier Milei’s election.

image.caption: Pelu, played by Octavio Bertone, in The Night Is Fading Away.

sources.originalTitle: The Night Is Fading Away review – hypnotic homage to cinema as a force for public good

segments.body: Set in Córdoba, Argentina, The Night Is Fading Away follows Pelu, a cinema projectionist reassigned as a night watchman after city budget cuts. He leaves his cramped rental and secretly lives at the theatre, where he welcomes an unemployed roommate, an ageing drifter and a sex worker who streams her shows from the building.

segments.title: Cinephilia beyond the screen
segments.body: The group watch films by directors including Jean Renoir, Yasujiro Ozu and Robert Bresson, but the review says their love of cinema is not simply a retreat into nostalgia. In the political climate after Milei’s 2023 election, the characters’ acts of vandalism turn the commercial space into a commune and a basis for action.

content.headline: Ben Affleck’s account reopens the story of Justice League’s troubled handover
content.shortHeadline: Ben Affleck’s remarks reopen Justice League’s history
content.standfirst: Affleck says Warner Bros used Zack Snyder’s family tragedy as an excuse to replace him on Justice League. The claim adds a new and serious dimension to a franchise story long framed around competing cuts and studio choices.

image.caption: Ben Affleck as Batman in Justice League.

sources.originalTitle: A Zack Snyder DC Universe might not have been such a bad thing, after all

segments.body: Ben Affleck has described the Justice League reshoots as the lowest point of his career and criticised the circumstances of Zack Snyder’s departure after his daughter’s death. Affleck alleged the studio used the family tragedy to justify replacing Snyder; the account is attributed to his interview on the Happy Sad Confused podcast.

segments.title: A franchise at a crossroads
segments.body: The commentary places Affleck’s allegation against the film’s already turbulent history, including Joss Whedon’s reshoots, Ray Fisher’s allegations of abusive conduct and Gal Gadot’s claim that Whedon threatened her career. Whedon denied the allegations. The piece argues that the handover may have weakened DC’s shared-film ambitions, while acknowledging that a Snyder-led alternative was no guarantee of success.

content.headline: Vampire Carnival has striking style but little beneath its love triangle
content.shortHeadline: Vampire Carnival’s atmosphere outpaces its story
content.standfirst: A grieving young woman is drawn into the world of a vampire carnival, where two performers compete for her attention. The review enjoys the film’s visual flair but finds its characters and conflicts underdeveloped.

image.caption: Pauline Chávez and Corrado Martini in Vampire Carnival.

sources.originalTitle: Vampire Carnival review – it’s Twilight at the fairground as abs run wild in pointy-toothed tug of war

segments.body: Gemma visits a carnival with her friends and discovers that its performers are vampires who follow a rule against killing without consent. Two men, the gentle Sebastian and her estranged ex Eric, pull her into a love triangle. The review praises the directors’ visual set pieces, including a tracking shot through the fair and a confrontation in a hall of mirrors.

segments.title: A conflict left in the shadows
segments.body: The film’s mood and good looks do not fully compensate for a story that shifts between treating Eric as a tragic figure and a dangerous loose cannon. The review finds the disagreement over vampire conduct underexplored and says the backstories do not prepare the ground for the ending.

content.headline: Fourteen film flops that deserve another look
content.shortHeadline: From The Thing to Babylon: 14 flops worth revisiting
content.standfirst: A list prompted by Digger’s poor box office makes the case for films whose reputations changed with time, from The Thing and Dune to Dredd and Babylon.

image.caption: Films that flopped on release but later found admirers.

sources.originalTitle: The 14 spectacular film flops that are actually worth watching

segments.body: The collection ranges from films that were misunderstood on release to ambitious projects whose failures became part of their legend. The Thing arrived amid a turn towards feel-good blockbusters; David Lynch’s Dune was shaped by a director who later disowned it; and Last Action Hero’s self-aware humour looks less out of place in retrospect.

segments.title: Failure is not the final verdict
segments.body: Other picks include Heaven’s Gate, Cloud Atlas, Dredd and Babylon: films whose unevenness or commercial disappointment does not erase their visual ambition or pleasures. The list uses Digger as a starting point for a broader reminder that box-office performance and later cultural standing do not always match.

content.headline: Galaxy Quest makes a warm-hearted case for taking fandom seriously
content.shortHeadline: Galaxy Quest finds kindness in its science-fiction parody
content.standfirst: The 1999 comedy sends a cast of washed-up television actors into a real interstellar crisis. Its affectionate jokes about fandom give way to a story about commitment, community and the power of make-believe.

image.caption: The cast of Galaxy Quest, including Tim Allen, Alan Rickman and Sigourney Weaver.

sources.originalTitle: ‘A beautiful dismantling of cynicism’: why Galaxy Quest is my feelgood movie

segments.body: In Galaxy Quest, aliens mistake a cancelled science-fiction show for historical fact and enlist its actors to help them. The film plays with genre conventions and television’s old-fashioned effects, but the essay argues that its affection for the fans is just as important as its parody.

segments.title: The joke is never on the fans
segments.body: The Thermians’ earnest belief in the show forces the actors to take their roles seriously, while a young fan helps save the day. The essay sees that as the film’s kindest idea: stories can matter to people even when outsiders think the costumes, lore or performances are silly.

content.headline: How Come Dine With Me made dinner-party awkwardness great television
content.shortHeadline: The people, not the food, made Come Dine With Me
content.standfirst: The show’s creator and narrator recall how a badly cooked dinner inspired a long-running format. Their account reveals the show’s carefully maintained balance between affectionate teasing and humiliation.

image.caption: A moment from Come Dine With Me.

sources.originalTitle: ‘Someone served sushi off a guy’s naked chest!’ How we made Come Dine With Me

segments.body: Come Dine With Me began after an executive producer’s disastrous attempt at a dinner party. The idea grew into a competition in which strangers take turns hosting, but Channel 4’s insistence that contestants be competent cooks helped shape the eventual format. A name change, a more conversational narrator and a focus on the guests made it something different from a straightforward food contest.

segments.title: The joke has a boundary
segments.body: The creator says the programme aims to puncture pomposity without sneering at contestants. Dave Lamb describes using the same principle for his voiceover: he avoids saying something he would not say to a participant’s face. The show’s creator credits its longevity to the ordinary people around the table, while Lamb says its appeal lies in watching how people live and feed themselves.

content.headline: Sebastian Croft brings heartbreak and ambition to his first music EP
content.shortHeadline: Sebastian Croft moves from Traitors fame to songwriting
content.standfirst: The actor’s time on Celebrity Traitors introduced him to a wider audience, but his forthcoming EP is built from songs he has written since childhood and shaped by a painful first breakup.

image.caption: Sebastian Croft, actor and singer-songwriter.

sources.originalTitle: Celebrity Traitors’ Sebastian Croft: ‘It was scary – the first time I’m being me’

segments.body: Sebastian Croft says Celebrity Traitors was the first time he felt he was appearing as himself rather than playing a character. The actor, known for roles including Heartstopper and Game of Thrones, has also been writing songs since childhood; he says the forthcoming EP The Great Forever marks a long-delayed move into music.

segments.title: Songs from a difficult chapter
segments.body: Croft says his first serious breakup in 2023 became the catalyst for the EP, which he spent three years refining. Its songs turn uncertainty and hurt into indie pop, from the dream-pop of “Pretty People” to “Tokyo”, which condenses conflicted feeling into the line “F**k you, but I hope you’re alright.” He says he wants to pursue music all the way to headlining Glastonbury.

content.headline: The Split Up brings a British Asian family into the drama’s centre
content.shortHeadline: The Split Up makes a new family its centre
content.standfirst: The BBC drama relocates its family-law battles to Manchester and introduces a predominantly British Asian cast. Its creators and lead actor describe how the spin-off aims to widen representation while keeping the original’s appetite for relationship drama.

image.caption: Ritu Arya in The Split Up.

sources.originalTitle: The Split is back – with a twist

segments.body: The Split Up follows Aria Kishan, a barrister expecting to take over her father’s firm, until her mother’s death changes his succession plans. The series keeps the high-stakes divorce cases and family conflicts of The Split but centres a new family in Manchester, led by Ritu Arya and Sanjeev Bhaskar.

segments.title: Representation in ordinary lives
segments.body: Writer Ursula Rani Sarma says she wanted British Asian characters living everyday lives, rather than being defined by a narrow set of familiar plotlines. The series’ executive producer, Abi Morgan, says the spin-off retains the original’s focus on family and romantic turmoil while giving a new team room to shape its own version.

content.headline: Why The Celebrity Traitors is struggling to replace its early chaos
content.shortHeadline: The Celebrity Traitors needs players willing to deceive
content.standfirst: An early Traitor’s dramatic mistake gave the series a thrilling opening, but a critic argues that subsequent contestants have been too cautious and media-trained to sustain the game’s central pleasures.

image.caption: Maya Jama in The Celebrity Traitors.

sources.originalTitle: The Celebrity Traitors has lost its spark – and I know exactly why

segments.body: The review says the current series has lost momentum since Richard E Grant, newly made a Traitor, revealed his role almost immediately and was banished. It argues that the celebrity contestants’ awareness of their public images has made them reluctant to take the risks and play the villains that the format needs.

segments.title: Politeness versus play
segments.body: The critic points to Traitors James Acaster and Hannah Fry as examples of players who avoid bold deception, and contrasts their restraint with the mischief of the previous series’ winner, Alan Carr. This is a review’s assessment of the show’s performance so far, not a claim that the contestants have all approached the game in the same way.

content.headline: Gnomes finds fun in a town overrun by murderous garden ornaments
content.shortHeadline: Gnomes turns a garden-ornament apocalypse into fun
content.standfirst: A small-town police team faces a gnome-led killing spree in this six-part Australian horror-comedy. The review likes its pulpy energy and cast, even if the biggest mayhem takes time to arrive.

image.caption: Asa Butterfield in the horror-comedy series Gnomes.

sources.originalTitle: Gnomes review – Asa Butterfield takes on murderous garden ornaments in pulpy horror-comedy

segments.body: In Nompton, a festival awakens an ancient evil and murderous garden gnomes descend on the town. The police, already facing cuts, are unprepared for the crisis. The review praises the series’ knowingly pulpy tone, its dark-stormy-night opening and the mix of local officials, police officers and teenagers drawn into the action.

segments.title: A slow build with a playful payoff
segments.body: The review says the show takes a few episodes to reach its full mayhem, but finds the build entertaining and the cast well judged. Asa Butterfield gives his character the right degree of false confidence, while the direction and midnight-movie look keep the absurd premise lively.

content.headline: Sarah Solemani brings class and personal loss to new drama The Party
content.shortHeadline: Sarah Solemani’s The Party looks at class and ambition
content.standfirst: The actor, writer and showrunner adapted Elizabeth Day’s novel for television, drawing on her long interest in Britain’s class system. She also reflects on bereavement, creative rejection and how #MeToo changed her experience of film sets.

image.caption: Sarah Solemani, actor, writer and showrunner of The Party.

sources.originalTitle: Sarah Solemani: ‘I performed at my mum’s hospice bed two weeks before she died’

segments.body: The Party centres on a birthday gathering where working-class journalist Martin and Tory politician Ben meet amid a secret and a clash of social worlds. Sarah Solemani plays Martin’s pregnant wife, Lucy, and says she initially tried to leave the role because she was also writing and running the series.

segments.title: Writing from experience
segments.body: Solemani says she has long struggled to get stories about British class made and was drawn to the novel’s character crossing those boundaries. She also recalls losing her mother at 16 and describes #MeToo as having dismantled parts of an old Hollywood system, including the conduct of dangerous men on sets.

content.headline: Ellie Taylor on hosting Strictly’s spin-off and adapting to change
content.shortHeadline: Ellie Taylor wants Strictly viewers to enjoy the change
content.standfirst: The comedian has taken over It Takes Two after auditioning for the main Strictly presenting job. She discusses viewer criticism, the appeal of leaning into the show’s camp humour and the demands of a packed presenting schedule.

image.caption: Ellie Taylor, presenter of It Takes Two.

sources.originalTitle: Ellie Taylor on the Strictly backlash: ‘People don’t like change’

segments.body: Ellie Taylor says hosting It Takes Two is a dream job, combining her enthusiasm for Strictly with years of stand-up and presenting. After viewers objected to a panel without professional dancers, she says the programme was already planning to bring them on and welcomed the audience’s engagement.

segments.title: The job she got
segments.body: Taylor auditioned for the main Saturday-night show but says she has made peace with not getting it. She argues that people can be resistant to change and urges viewers to focus on the dancing, while balancing the spin-off with a Radio 2 hosting role.

content.headline: Rainbow Six Tactics brings the shooter’s planning into turn-based play
content.shortHeadline: Rainbow Six Tactics turns preparation into the action
content.standfirst: Ubisoft Paris moves from Mario and Rabbids to a tactical spin-off of Rainbow Six Siege. Its developers argue that careful preparation, rather than speed or brutality, makes the series a natural fit for turn-based strategy.

image.caption: A scene from Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics.

sources.originalTitle: From Mario to machine guns: how Ubisoft Paris made Tom Clancy’s Rainbow Six Tactics

segments.body: Rainbow Six Tactics swaps the studio’s colourful Mario and Rabbids world for tactical operations built around the Rainbow Six series. In a hands-on demo set in Nigeria, a four-person team uses drones, explosives and coordinated movement to breach a guarded warehouse, retaining the tension of the real-time shooter in a turn-based structure.

segments.title: More than one way through
segments.body: Creative director Elie Benhamou says the series’ emphasis on preparation and consequential decisions makes it well suited to tactics. Players can approach missions in different ways with 15 operators, and can arrest some enemies rather than kill them. The studio also describes the wider tactical-sim genre as niche but still active.

content.headline: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse pairs gothic spectacle with demanding action
content.shortHeadline: Belmont’s Curse is thrilling, if uneven, vampire-hunting
content.standfirst: Rose Belmont fights to free Paris from demons in a new entry that prioritises fast, punishing combat over the series’ familiar exploration. The review finds real invention, though not every stretch of the adventure earns its place.

image.caption: Rose Belmont in Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse.

sources.originalTitle: Castlevania: Belmont’s Curse review – every fantastical vampire-hunting vision is fulfilled

segments.body: Belmont’s Curse puts Rose Belmont, daughter of series regulars Trevor Belmont and Sypha Belnades, in a demonic Paris. Its battles are frantic and demanding, with even minor enemies able to inflict heavy damage. The review finds the shift towards quick, skill-based combat a notable departure from earlier Castlevania games.

segments.title: A world of uneven challenges
segments.body: Exploration leans on difficult platforming rooms, traps and tools rather than the series’ usual emphasis on backtracking and secret-hunting. A castle library offers clever puzzles, but other areas rely on repetitive combat. The review says the game improves after Rose is forced to confront her family legacy, though it does not match the strongest of its contemporary peers.

content.headline: End of Abyss makes survival horror feel like a tiny, dark diorama
content.shortHeadline: End of Abyss turns survival horror into a dollhouse
content.standfirst: This overhead horror game stages its monsters and ruined rooms like a miniature world, with clear echoes of Resident Evil and The Thing. The review praises its visual control but finds the extended backtracking draining.

image.caption: The small-scale world of End of Abyss.

sources.originalTitle: End of Abyss review – a creepy dollhouse take on Resident Evil and The Thing

segments.body: End of Abyss shrinks a decaying facility into a foggy, top-down world of carefully arranged rooms and bodies. The fixed perspective makes each scene feel like a diorama, allowing monsters to emerge from darkness just beyond the player’s attention. The review describes its best moments as compact, unsettling versions of classic survival-horror scares.

segments.title: When the map becomes a maze
segments.body: The game adds interconnected routes and exploration to its survival-horror foundations, but the reviewer finds the combination awkward. Slow movement, a confusing map and indistinct-looking rooms lead to repeated backtracking, and the staged scares lose their effect on repeated visits. The visual style remains strong even as the game outlasts its welcome.

content.headline: Replaying Modern Warfare 2 gave a father and son a new co-op story
content.shortHeadline: A father and son return to the game they first played together
content.standfirst: Seventeen years after they first tackled its co-op missions, a father and his grown son return to Modern Warfare 2. Their reunion becomes a story about teamwork, time and the pleasure of playing without pressure.

image.caption: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 2, the game a father and son played together.

sources.originalTitle: Playing video games with my 22-year-old son has brought me to tears

segments.body: The writer and his 22-year-old son revisit the Special Ops missions they began playing together when the boy was five. Their old habits remain: the father moves cautiously and scouts ahead, while his son charges in. After repeated failures, they find a compromise and finally complete missions they never managed as a child and parent.

segments.title: A shared memory in the making
segments.body: The game gives them a familiar reason to spend long evenings together, but the piece is less about mastery than about enjoying the time. The son tells his father he will remember the sessions as some of their best times; the writer reflects on the relief of playing without the usual pressures of work, parenthood and ambition.

content.headline: Blood antibody patterns may signal inflammatory bowel disease years early
content.shortHeadline: Blood signals may flag bowel disease years before diagnosis
content.standfirst: A study found immune patterns associated with Crohn’s disease and ulcerative colitis in blood samples taken up to a decade before diagnosis. The findings are promising, but the researchers say this is not yet a clinical test.

image.caption: Research into blood antibody patterns could help identify people at risk of inflammatory bowel disease earlier.

sources.originalTitle: Warning signs could predict inflammatory bowel disease a decade before diagnosis

segments.body: Researchers examined 2,000 blood samples from 500 US military personnel, including people who later developed Crohn’s disease or ulcerative colitis. In those who went on to develop Crohn’s, antibodies to Epstein-Barr virus were more common; those who developed ulcerative colitis showed a different pattern, including antibodies to a protein made by the body.

segments.title: A research lead, not a test
segments.body: Some antibody differences were visible as much as 10 years before diagnosis, and the signal was strongest in people who later developed more severe Crohn’s disease. The study shows an association, not that infection causes IBD, and the findings need confirmation in other groups. A gastroenterology professor not involved in the work called the techniques a research tool, not something ready for clinical use.

perspectives.body: The study’s lead author, Dr Arno Bourgonje, said the immune system may leave warning signs years before symptoms appear, but stressed that the results are not yet a test that can predict whether an individual will become ill.

content.headline: Four popular anti-ageing claims face a challenge from a longevity researcher
content.shortHeadline: A longevity researcher challenges four anti-ageing claims
content.standfirst: Oxford demographer Saul Newman argues that evidence behind claims about centenarians, “Blue Zones”, telomeres and young-blood treatments is weak or misleading. Some of his conclusions are contested, and the article is an expert’s critique, not a review of scientific consensus.

image.caption: Oxford demographer Saul Newman, who criticises claims made in some anti-ageing research.

sources.originalTitle: I’m a longevity expert. These four anti-ageing myths are junk science

segments.body: Newman says records of extreme old age are often unreliable, making it hard to draw lessons from centenarians. He also challenges the evidence that so-called Blue Zones have unusually long-lived populations, arguing that the idea has been commercialised and rests on poor data. A company associated with the Blue Zones concept says its programmes are scientifically validated and that Newman’s work has been disproven.

segments.title: What the evidence does—and doesn’t—show
segments.body: Newman argues that telomeres, protective structures at chromosome ends, are not a simple route to extending life: later research has complicated early optimism about the theory. He also points to the lack of proven benefit and potential risks in young-plasma transfusions; the US Food and Drug Administration has warned that the practice has no proven clinical benefit for preventing ageing or memory loss.

perspectives.body: The article presents Newman’s sceptical assessment of several areas of longevity research. It also includes a response from a Blue Zones representative, who says Newman’s criticism has been disproven, and a 2015 paper cited by Nobel laureate Elizabeth Blackburn on telomere biology’s roles in human disease.

content.headline: UK review warns ADHD diagnoses may soon exceed population estimates in some
content.shortHeadline: UK review flags rising ADHD diagnoses and overdiagnosis risk
content.standfirst: A government-commissioned review says NHS diagnoses among some groups of young people are approaching or exceeding estimates of how common ADHD is. It warns of a possible shift towards overdiagnosis, but says current evidence does not prove it is happening at scale.

image.caption: The review examines rising rates of ADHD and autism diagnoses among young people.

sources.originalTitle: The four reasons why ADHD experts fear the UK is heading towards overdiagnosis

segments.body: The review found that 5% of teenage boys had an ADHD diagnosis last year, up from 2% a decade earlier; among girls of the same age, the rate rose from 0.5% to 2.5%. It says diagnosis rates for ADHD and autism in some groups are approaching or already exceeding estimates of prevalence, while waiting lists continue to grow.

segments.title: A warning, not a verdict
segments.body: The authors say the figures do not establish that overdiagnosis is already occurring at scale. They point to challenges including subjective assessments, broader diagnostic definitions, greater awareness and incentives linked to support. The review’s lead author called the findings a warning sign, while other contributors say the balance of risks may be changing; underdiagnosis and misdiagnosis remain concerns too.

perspectives.body: Professor Peter Fonagy, who led the review’s authors, described the findings as a warning about overdiagnosis rather than a definitive conclusion that it is occurring.

content.headline: Light-activated gene therapy partially restores vision in a small study
content.shortHeadline: Light-activated gene therapy partly restored vision in six patients
content.standfirst: In a study of 10 people with severe vision loss from retinitis pigmentosa, six had meaningful improvement after treatment using a gene that makes retinal cells respond to amber light. The approach is experimental and did not restore normal sight.

image.caption: Optogenetics uses light to control the activity of nerve cells.

sources.originalTitle: A cure for blindness is coming

segments.body: The treatment introduces a gene into the retina so that some nerve cells respond to amber light. Patients wear glasses that convert ordinary light into amber shades. In the reported study, six of 10 participants had meaningful improvement after three months, including being able to pick up a cup from a table; they could not distinguish faces.

segments.title: A wider research prospect
segments.body: The approach is part of optogenetics, which uses light to control nerve cells. Researchers are also investigating possible applications in pain, epilepsy and hearing, but those uses remain at different stages of development. For hearing, for example, optogenetic implants have so far been tested in animals, and the gene therapy would need to be shown safe.

content.headline: Hotter, drier summers are prompting research into new UK food crops
content.shortHeadline: Could drought-tolerant crops reshape what UK growers plant?
content.standfirst: Researchers are testing crops such as lupins and chickpeas that may cope better with hotter, drier summers. They could broaden UK food production, but researchers say more work is needed on where varieties will grow and how pests and disease may affect them.

image.caption: A lupin bhaji made with flour from a drought-tolerant crop being explored for future UK growing.

sources.originalTitle: The protein-packed superfoods of the future – that you could grow in your garden

segments.body: A research group at Southampton is exploring crops that may be better suited to a changing climate. Lupin beans are drought-tolerant and can be milled into flour; chickpeas are already grown by a small number of UK farmers and may also cope with dry conditions. Researchers are working with chefs and food businesses to test possible uses.

segments.title: Adaptation has limits
segments.body: The researchers say they need to establish which varieties suit different parts of the UK and how pests and diseases could affect them before farmers plant them at scale. Warmer conditions may also help some crops while late spring frosts still threaten fruit blossom. The Royal Horticultural Society expects some growing patterns to shift north, but the winners and losers are not yet certain.

content.headline: Four European mobile carriers consider a joint bid for satellite phone service
content.shortHeadline: European carriers consider satellite service to rival Starlink
content.standfirst: Deutsche Telekom, Orange, Telefónica and Vodafone say they are considering a joint bid for spectrum to support direct-to-device satellite service. They would build ground infrastructure, while a satellite partner has yet to be selected.

sources.originalTitle: Major European mobile carriers are teaming up for a ‘direct’ satellite program without Starlink

segments.body: The four operators have signed a letter of intent to explore a joint bid for spectrum that could support a European direct-to-device satellite service. They say it could extend coverage in underserved areas and strengthen the resilience of public networks. The companies would handle ground infrastructure, rather than investing directly in the satellite constellation.

The project still needs a satellite partner, which has not been announced, and the carriers say they are considering a bid rather than announcing a completed service. The plan follows a US collaboration among major mobile operators and comes as the EU considers reserving spectrum for local satellite services.

content.headline: Children as young as five are being targeted by online groomers, police warn
content.shortHeadline: Police warn online grooming is reaching children as young as five
content.standfirst: Police and child-safety groups say grooming is happening through social media, messaging and gaming platforms. Their advice to parents is to keep communication open and make clear that children can ask for help without blame.

image.caption: Police warn that children may be targeted through social media, messaging and gaming platforms.

sources.originalTitle: Snapchat and Instagram grooming becoming 'easier'

segments.body: Avon and Somerset Police say children as young as five can be targeted online. The NSPCC recorded 756 sexual communication offences involving children in the South West in 2024–25, more than double the figure when the offence was introduced seven years ago. Snapchat was mentioned in 324 of the charity’s counselling sessions about online sexual abuse during 2025–26, followed by TikTok and Instagram.

segments.title: Keep a route to help open
segments.body: Police and the NSPCC advise parents to talk with children about their online lives and respond with warmth if a child discloses abuse. Police officer Andri Nicolau cautions against taking devices away or banning platforms, which could make children feel at fault. The NSPCC says children should know they have a trusted adult to turn to.

content.headline: Australian report calls for stronger privacy rules as employers use AI to track
content.shortHeadline: Australia urged to strengthen privacy rules for workplace monitoring
content.standfirst: A University of Technology Sydney institute says employers increasingly use tools including CCTV, keystroke tracking and AI systems to monitor workers, often without their knowledge. It wants workplace laws to require fairer, more transparent use.

image.caption: Workplace monitoring can include CCTV, tracking messages and monitoring workers’ computer activity.

sources.originalTitle: Calls to strengthen workplace privacy in Australia as employers turn to AI to track staff

segments.body: The Human Technology Institute says workplace monitoring is appearing across retail, offices, factories and delivery work. It cited a supermarket cashier who received a final written warning after an AI system flagged errors in about 0.18% of scans, and young fast-food workers who feared cameras were monitoring phone use in changing rooms.

segments.title: Proposed safeguards
segments.body: The institute wants workplace laws to require monitoring to be fair and reasonable, with employers consulting workers and explaining what data they collect. It also recommends a dedicated route for privacy complaints and powers to restrict surveillance products that pose unacceptable risks. A poll cited in the report found 43% of Australians knew some employers used monitoring technology, but only 9% knew it was used in their own workplace.

perspectives.body: The institute’s co-director, Edward Santow, said transparency is necessary but not sufficient, and called for a test of whether workplace monitoring is appropriate.

content.headline: AI coding tools are helping musicians rewrite the firmware in old gear
content.shortHeadline: AI is helping musicians unlock new features in old music gear
content.standfirst: Hobbyists are using coding assistants to build custom firmware for synthesizers, samplers and effects pedals, adding features that once required specialist skills. The projects can revive older equipment, but unofficial updates may contain bugs or damage devices.

sources.originalTitle: Vibe coding is turning the music gear world upside down

segments.body: Musicians have used AI coding tools to add features to devices from brands including Elektron, Roland and Zoom. One community project has expanded the capabilities of Yamaha’s low-cost FM-1 synthesizer with new sound engines and sequencing options. Developers say coding assistants have made experiments possible in days that might once have taken weeks or months.

segments.title: The risks of unofficial updates
segments.body: Custom firmware is often less thoroughly tested than a manufacturer’s release and can cause devices to malfunction. Elektron warns that modifications can brick equipment or create problems when official software is updated. M-Vave, by contrast, has announced an open-source firmware and tools for its FM-1, signalling support for community development.

content.headline: Microsoft exits UK AI data-centre project after power supply delay
content.shortHeadline: Microsoft leaves UK AI data-centre project delayed until the 2030s
